archetypes.hoarder: You're protecting the budget extremely well — but the safety you're hoarding isn't turning into growth. An idle team costs just as much as risk does, just slower and less visibly.
archetypes.generalist: You don't lean hard in any one direction — not big risks, not tight defense, not deep focus. That's not inherently bad, but check: is this a deliberate balance, or did you just never settle on a focus?
archetypes.firefighter: You react to crises that have already caught fire more often than you prevent them. Your team and budget get attention once it's already late — try responding to early warning signs next time, not the fire itself.
archetypes.cautious_builder: You keep the budget safe almost all the time — it shows. The question is whether you're paying for that safety with lost growth: caution taken to the extreme costs just as much as risk, it's just harder to notice.
archetypes.gambler: You go for big bets — fast growth, minimal safety margin. Sometimes it pays off spectacularly, sometimes it costs a lot. Before repeating this in a real company, ask yourself: was the risk deliberate, or were you just rushing?
archetypes.people_first: Your team is in good shape — morale is high, turnover is low. But look at your growth and cashflow numbers: are you trading speed and growth for team comfort more than necessary?
archetypes.specialist: You're sticking to one domain or niche and clearly building reputation there. It works — until that niche cools off. Is it time to start thinking about diversifying, or is it too early?
archetypes.insufficient_data: Too early to judge — you haven't made enough decisions yet for a reliable read. Play a bit more before we draw conclusions.
archetypes.inactive: Low activity this session — scores stay capped until you hire, assign, and deliver more consistently.

onboarding.title: How to play
onboarding.intro: You're running a company. Hire people, take on client work, keep the business alive — and grow it — over 4 quarters.
onboarding.hiring: Each candidate has a role and a skill tier (Junior/Middle/Senior). Higher tiers cost more but perform better. You can re-roll the candidate pool if none of them fit.
onboarding.assigning: Leads and projects need to be matched to the right person — some require a specific specialization. If nobody available is a good match, you can either assign anyway or wait for a better fit. Both are valid choices — waiting has a cost too.
onboarding.team: Employees have morale. Give a bonus to lift it. Ignore it too long, and people leave. You can also let someone go if they're not working out — severance applies.
onboarding.risk: Some industries are more heavily regulated than others. Compliance reviews can happen during the game, and they can carry a financial penalty.
onboarding.growth: Build more desks, open new office rooms, and expand your team as revenue allows.
onboarding.end: You'll get two reports: your company's financial results (P&L), and a Manager Report — a breakdown of how you made your decisions, not just what the outcome was.
